summary: Specifies three tools needed for debugging networks that use CLNP: a ping or OSI Echo function, a traceroute that uses that echo, and a routing table dump.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1574 lists the minimum set of debugging tools for networks that use ISO 8473, the OSI connectionless network protocol. It requires every host and router to offer a ping function, a traceroute function and a way to print its routing tables, so that operators have a common way to find network faults. It also fixes a shared file format that maps host names to OSI addresses.

questions: what tools are required for clns
subtitle: Three required tools for debugging ISO 8473 networks: an echo function, a traceroute and a routing table dump.

tldr.problem: Network managers adding OSI protocols to what had been a mostly TCP/IP Internet found that network layer debugging tools were almost nonexistent, and the ones that existed did not work together across implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The memo requires an echo function (ping), a traceroute built on that echo function, and a dump of the routing tables on every host and router that provides OSI service, plus a fixed file format for mapping host names to OSI addresses.
tldr.outcome: It set the minimum tool set for CLNP networks and fixed a shared format for the host name to NSAP address file so that mapping could be copied between sites.

today: RFC 1574 is an Informational memo published in February 1994. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it describes the debugging tools required on hosts and routers that provide OSI service for the Internet, using ISO 8473 (CLNP).

sections.title: Why Debugging Tools Were Needed
sections.content:
Network managers who were adding OSI protocols to an Internet that had been mostly TCP/IP found that tools for debugging the network layer barely existed. Where such tools did exist, different implementations did not work together, so one vendor's packet was not understood by another.

The memo therefore defines a minimum support level. Every router (intermediate system) and host (end system) that provides OSI service for the Internet must make three mechanisms available: a ping or OSI Echo function, a traceroute function that uses that Echo function, and a routing table dump. These three functions are the basic tool set for the OSI network layer for the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo requires three tools on every host and router that speaks OSI: a ping, a traceroute and a way to print the routing table. Without them there was no common way to debug a network problem, and tools from different suppliers did not work together.

sections.title: Ping and the OSI Echo Function
sections.content:
The echo mechanism comes from RFC 1575, which defines two new values for the type code option field in the header of an ISO 8473 packet: 1E (hex) for the echo-request selector and 1F (hex) for the echo-response selector. A node that supports ISO 8473 but not these two values must send back an error packet if the ERROR report flag is set in the packet it received.

To support ping, all end systems and intermediate systems must implement the long term echo function of RFC 1575 and must also set the ERROR report flag in the ISO 8473 header. Setting that flag is what lets a compliant node test a node that is not compliant: a non-compliant node that receives the echo-request must attempt to return an ISO 8473 error packet to the sender, which shows that the destination is reachable.

The ping utility must report the round trip time of each packet, plus the average, minimum and maximum round trip time over several ping packets, and it must report the error code to the user when an error packet is received.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping sends a CLNP packet marked as an echo request and waits for the echo reply. The reply normally comes from the target, but the memo also makes a target that does not support the echo function send back an error packet instead, so a reply of either kind shows the target is reachable.

sections.title: Traceroute and the Lifetime Field
sections.content:
The trace works like ping but uses the Lifetime field of the ISO 8473 packet, which serves the same function as the Time To Live field does in an IP packet. A node cannot forward an ISO 8473 packet whose Lifetime is zero, and it returns an error packet to the originator when the ERROR report flag is set.

An echo-request sent with a Lifetime of 1 is expired by the first hop, which answers with an error packet whose code is A0 (Lifetime Expired while Data Unit in Transit) or A1 (Lifetime Expired during Re-assembly). If the first hop does not support the echo-request type field, the code is B0 (Unsupported Option not Specified). The originator then sends a packet with a Lifetime of 2: the first hop decrements it and, because it is still greater than zero, forwards the packet, and the second hop decrements it to zero and sends the error packet. The sequence repeats until the remote host answers with an echo-response, until a node answers with the B0 error, or until the destination address is reported as unreachable (80) or unknown (81).

The memo also describes a loose source route form of the trace, which requires setting the source routing option with the partial source routing parameter. Two errors end that form of the trace: 92 (Unknown Address in Source Routeing Field) and 93 (Path not Acceptable). A traceroute utility should report the identity of the systems that make up the path (called Network Entity Titles, or NETs, in OSI), the ping times for each hop, the error codes received in response to echo-request packets, and any other error conditions it encounters.
sections.plainLanguage: Traceroute finds the path one hop at a time. It sends a probe with a lifetime of 1, so the first router on the path gives up and reports back. It then raises the lifetime to 2, so the second router reports back, and repeats until it reaches the destination or the path breaks.

sections.title: Routing Table Dump and SNMP Variables
sections.content:
Each OSI host or router must be able to dump any of its routing tables. The tables may have been filled from ES-IS information, from static entries, from IS-IS, from IDRP, or from any other source. The dump must be available through some out-of-band mechanism, and the memo suggests a show osi routes command whose options select the source: a for all routes, esis for ES-IS routes, isis for IS-IS routes, idrp for IDRP routes, static for static routes and other for routes from other sources.

The routing tables should also be available over SNMP or CMIP. The CMIP variables are outside the scope of the memo, so it specifies the two RFC 1238 CLNS MIB variables that must be available over SNMP: clnpAddrTable, which holds the addresses of the interfaces, and clnpRoutingTable, which holds the OSI routes in the system routing table. The memo repeats their ASN.1 syntax for reference and states that RFC 1238 remains the authoritative source for the MIB definitions.

The memo also notes that not all the information requested is available through the CLNS MIB today, that additional work on a CLNS MIB is anticipated, and that this document is expected to be updated with the additional MIB variables once they exist, for example to collect the ES-IS cache.
sections.plainLanguage: Each machine must also be able to print the routes it knows about, filtered by where the route came from: ES-IS, IS-IS, IDRP, or a manually configured entry. The same information is published over SNMP in two tables, one for interface addresses and one for routes.

sections.title: The osi host.txt File
sections.content:
The OSI address format allows addresses to be 20 bytes. In the long term a directory service, either DNS or the OSI Directory service (X.500), will provide the mapping from host name to address. Getting such a service working over OSI may require an OSI pathway to be set up first, so most host and router systems use a fixed table for the name to NSAP mapping in order to get OSI working at all. Each implementation used a different format, so this section defines a fixed format so that the initial name to NSAP mapping files can be shared throughout the Internet.

A host or router supporting CLNS must support an osi host.txt file, and NSAP addresses in any OSI address information must use that format. Each line is an NSAP address followed by a sequence of names: <NSAP Address> <name1> <name2> ...<name>. The NSAP octets are written in hexadecimal, and dots may be inserted to help the reader. The dots must not be required for parsing, their position carries no significance other than making the address easier to read, and a file must be able to handle their insertion.

Two example addresses are given: one in GOSIP format, 47.0005.80ff.ff00.0000.0001.0001.0a0b.0c0d.0204.00, and one in ANSI format, 39.480f.8000.0500.0000.0001.0001.0a0b0c0d.0204.00, which shows the AFI and the NSEL octets on either end. The mapping must be available to the OSI Echo (Ping) function, the OSI traceroute function, and the router table lookup for CLNS routing information, and hosts and routers must also support the NSAP to name mapping through DNS or the OSI Directory service (X.500).
sections.plainLanguage: Before a directory service could map names to OSI addresses, each site kept its own table in its own format. This section fixes one format: each line holds an OSI address in hexadecimal, with optional dots for readability, followed by the names that address answers to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of the memo says only this: security issues are not discussed in it. Nothing in the document describes authentication, access control or any other protection for the echo function, the traceroute function or the routing table dump that it requires on every host and router.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. It describes no authentication or access control for the ping, traceroute and routing table functions it requires.
